messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 26
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Fisherman
  trauma_type: Torture
  pcl5: 37

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Auditory (Babies): Babies, Public Transport: Bus riding, Feeling Vulnerable: Feeling emotionally vulnerable
  Threat: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room, Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home, Noticing Weapons: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment
  Memory: Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage, Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Alex sits in the therapy room with a stillness that seems to cost him a great deal of effort. At twenty-six, his work as a fisherman has weathered his hands and face, but a different kind of tension now pulls at the corners of his eyes and mouth. The story of the past eight months unfolds hesitantly. It began on a fishing trip abroad, a misunderstanding in a port town that escalated with terrifying speed. He was mistaken for someone else, dragged from a bar, and held for two days in a windowless basement. His captors wanted information he didn't have, and their methods were designed to break him. They bound him to a metal chair, his arms wrenched behind his back, and for hours on end, they played a looping recording of babies wailing at a deafening volume, the high-pitched, frantic sounds drilling into his skull until he couldn't form a coherent thought. Between the noise, they would beat his back and ribs, the sharp, radiating pain a punctuation mark in the auditory assault.

When he was finally released and made it home, he believed the worst was over. But the basement came back with him. At first, it was the rage, a white-hot fury that would surge whenever he remembered the feeling of utter helplessness in that chair. He would be mending a net on the docks, his hands going through the familiar motions, when the memory would surface. His breath would catch, the phantom ache would blossom across his ribs, and his shoulders would instinctively tense and pull back, his body reenacting its bound position. The fury was so intense it felt like a physical force, and he would have to walk away from his crewmates, afraid of what he might say or do. The pain was just as real; a sharp, specific throb in his side that mirrored the kicks he’d endured, a ghost of the original injury that had long since healed.

His world began to shrink, reconfigured around a new and constant sense of threat. The bus he used to take to the harbor became an impossible space—the press of bodies, the lack of an escape route, the feeling of being trapped felt too much like the van that first took him. After one attempt where the closing doors sent a wave of panic through him so strong he had to force his way off at the next stop, he gave up, adding an hour-long walk to his pre-dawn commute. He finds no peace at home, either. He spends his evenings listening, certain that the groan of the house settling or the scrape of a branch against the window is the sound of someone trying the lock. He can only sit in the one chair in the living room that faces the door, his back pressed firmly against the wall. His wife, Sarah, doesn't understand why he can't relax, why he startles at every noise.

The triggers are everywhere, insidious and unpredictable. A few months ago, while shopping for groceries with Sarah, a baby started crying in the next aisle. The sound—piercing, desperate—hit him like a physical blow. The supermarket lights seemed to pulse, the air grew thick, and he was back in the dark, the wailing coming from the speakers. He dropped the basket and fled the store, leaving a bewildered Sarah behind. Since then, he has avoided any place where there might be children. This has made him a ghost at family gatherings and a stranger in his own neighborhood. His work, once a source of pride, has become a landscape of potential dangers. Every gaff hook, every filleting knife on the boat is no longer a tool but a weapon he can't stop cataloging in his mind.

He feels himself becoming a stranger to his wife. He can’t explain the terror to her, because the act of trying to be emotionally vulnerable, of trying to name the fear, is itself a trigger that brings the helplessness rushing back. He sees the worry and confusion in her eyes, but he can’t bridge the gap. The breaking point came last week. Sarah found him in the garage, standing rigid in the dark, his arms locked behind his back as if bound, his face a mask of silent fury. He was lost in a memory, and the sight terrified her. It was her fear, so palpable in the quiet garage, that finally pierced through his own. He is here now not because the rage has faded, but because he is afraid it will one day consume him entirely, leaving nothing of the man he used to be.
